title: Can full-batch first-order methods match SGD’s O(ε⁻²) generalization rate?
formal: Historical question, resolved negatively in the source’s dimension-independent sample setting: is there a family of full-batch first-order methods with n=O(ε⁻²) independent training examples and T=O(ε⁻²) oracle calls that guarantees expected population excess risk at most ε for every dimension d and every convex 1-Lipschitz stochastic loss on the Euclidean unit ball? All hidden constants must be independent of d and of the loss distribution. The later NeurIPS 2021 theorem rules this out: with sample count independent of d, general full-batch methods require Ω(ε⁻⁴) calls in the worst case. This conclusion concerns access solely to the empirical average; stochastic methods allowed to query individual examples already achieve the faster rate.
context:
An algorithm may fit the empirical average quickly while making poor predictions on new data. The target is the expected excess of the true risk, so a fast optimization guarantee for F_S alone does not answer it.

The COLT paper proves lower bounds for gradient descent and selected regularized variants, then asks whether another first-order method over the empirical risk can match the stochastic rate. Its context is essential: if individual-example gradients were allowed, SGD would already supply an affirmative answer.

The NeurIPS paper formalizes full-batch access and proves the Ω(ε⁻⁴) oracle lower bound without restricting the learner to ordinary gradient descent or to the span of previous gradients. Together with the known full-batch upper bound, it identifies the slower worst-case rate.

The lower-bound dimension can be polynomial in 2^n, the call budget and inverse accuracy. The theorem therefore does not claim the same obstruction at a fixed small dimension or when sample size may grow with dimension. It rules out a guarantee uniform across all dimensions at the desired dimension-independent sample scale.

For generalized-linear stochastic losses, a 2022 paper obtains the faster rate using unprojected gradient descent. Its abstract explicitly contrasts that restricted setting with the lower bound for general stochastic convex optimization. It does not overturn the original full-class resolution.
why: Separates statistical generalization under aggregate training-data access from learning with individual samples, establishing a fundamental limitation of full-batch optimization beyond particular update rules.
status_note: Matched the original question’s empirical-risk and dimension-independent sampling context to the complete model and Theorem 2.1 of the published NeurIPS paper; also read the full author version. Checked subsequent records through 12 September 2026. The theorem is a worst-case high-dimensional statement, not a claim about every convex instance or every oracle-access model; no independent proof audit or formal certificate is claimed.

progress.text: The COLT paper poses the possibility of an O(ε⁻²)-iteration general first-order empirical-risk method after proving bounds for specific gradient-descent variants.
The NeurIPS follow-up gives a general full-batch oracle lower bound of Ω(ε⁻⁴) when sample complexity is dimension-independent, resolving the question negatively in its intended setting.

sentences: The task is to minimize population risk for arbitrary convex Lipschitz losses on a unit ball.
A full-batch method sees only the value and averaged subgradient of one fixed empirical sample.
The source asks whether such a method can generalize in O(ε⁻²) calls using dimension-independent samples.
The later NeurIPS theorem requires Ω(ε⁻⁴) calls for general full-batch methods in this setting.
The negative resolution does not apply to individual-example access, fixed low-dimensional regimes or extra regularity assumptions.

references.authors: Idan Amir, Tomer Koren, Roi Livni
references.locator: Unresolved-question passage on page 10; PDF page 10

definitions: For each d≥1 let W={w∈ℝ^d:‖w‖₂≤1}. A loss f(w;z) is convex in w if f(θu+(1−θ)v;z)≤θf(u;z)+(1−θ)f(v;z) for θ∈[0,1], and is 1-Lipschitz if |f(u;z)−f(v;z)|≤‖u−v‖₂ for u,v∈W. Draw S=(z₁,…,z_n) independently from an unknown distribution D and keep this same sample throughout the computation. Population risk is F(w)=E_{z∼D}f(w;z), assumed finite; empirical risk is F_S(w)=(1/n)Σᵢf(w;zᵢ). A full-batch oracle queried at w∈W returns the exact pair (F_S(w),(1/n)Σᵢg(w;zᵢ)), where g(w;z) is a subgradient satisfying f(u;z)≥f(w;z)+⟨g(w;z),u−w⟩ for all u∈W. The subgradient selection for one example depends only on that example and w, not on the other training examples; use valid norm-at-most-one selections for the Lipschitz losses. The learner cannot inspect S or obtain individual-example values or gradients. Its next query and final output may be arbitrary measurable functions of previous oracle replies, d,n,ε and internal random coins independent of S. All queries and the output lie in W. There is no span restriction and no bound on intervening computation. Cost T counts full-batch oracle calls, not the n individual gradients used internally to form one reply; the bound is on the maximum number of calls. Accuracy means E_{S,coins}[F(ŵ)−min_{w∈W}F(w)]≤ε. An admissible positive result would have to work for every permitted loss distribution and subgradient oracle. Dimension-independent sample complexity means n is bounded by a function of ε alone, uniformly over d; the original optimal-sample target is O(ε⁻²). Losses need not be smooth or strongly convex.
answer_criterion: The published lower bound refutes the proposed dimension-independent O(ε⁻²)-call guarantee for full-batch first-order access. It applies to arbitrary adaptive randomized methods, including regularized or accelerated updates implementable through this oracle. An algorithm using individual training examples, querying outside W, assuming extra smoothness or taking a dimension-dependent number of samples addresses a different target.
